items.title: Biggest crash cause: missed risk
items.simple: The biggest cause of crashes is missing a risk. Keep looking ahead, to the sides and behind you. Know where other cars are. Watch for people walking and riding bikes.
items.official: The single biggest contributor to crashes is failing to identify a risk. Always know where other vehicles are positioned around you. You must look down the road, to the sides, and behind your vehicle. You must also be alert for unexpected events, especially pedestrians and bicyclists.

items.title: Headlights at 500-foot visibility
items.simple: Rain, fog, snow or sleet can make it hard to see. Can you see only 500 feet ahead? Then you must turn on your headlights. It is the law.
items.official: Virginia law requires motorists to use headlights during inclement weather such as rain, fog, snow or sleet when visibility is reduced to 500 feet.

items.title: Wipers on means headlights on
items.simple: Are your wipers on for bad weather? Then your headlights must be on too. Headlights help other drivers see you, even in the daytime.
items.official: You must use your headlights whenever you use your windshield wipers as a result of bad weather. Using headlights at all times, including during the day, increases your vehicle's visibility.

items.title: Headlights whenever it's hard to see
items.simple: You must use your headlights at night. Use them any other time it is hard to see, too.
items.official: You must use your headlights at night and at other times when it's hard to see.

items.title: Bad conditions: slow down first
items.simple: It is risky to drive when you can't see well. It is risky when rain, snow or ice covers the road. Your first move is to slow down. Then turn on your headlights.
items.official: Driving becomes hazardous when visibility is reduced or when the road surface is covered with rain, snow or ice. Reducing your speed should be your first response to decreased visibility and dangerous road conditions. Turn on your headlights.

items.title: Double your following distance
items.simple: Bad weather? Slick road? Leave twice your normal space behind the car ahead. More space gives you more time to stop.
items.official: Increase your space cushion by doubling your normal following distance.

items.title: Headlights from sunset to sunrise
items.simple: Turn on your headlights at sunset, as soon as it starts to get dark. Keep them on until sunrise. This helps other drivers see you.
items.official: At sunset, as soon as light begins to fade, turn on your headlights to make your vehicle more visible to others. You must use headlights from sunset to sunrise.
items.mnemonic: Sun goes down, lights go on.

items.title: Low beams in town, for oncoming
items.simple: Use low beams in cities and towns, unless the street has no lights. Is a car coming toward you? Switch to low beams so you don't blind the driver.
items.official: Use low-beams when driving in cities and towns, except on streets where there is no lighting. Switch to low-beams whenever you meet oncoming traffic to avoid blinding the other driver.

items.title: Following: low beams within 200 feet
items.simple: Are you driving behind a car at night? Once you are within 200 feet of it, use your low beams.
items.official: When following, use low-beams whenever you are within 200 feet of the vehicle ahead.
items.mnemonic: Behind a car: 200 feet. Car coming at you: 500 feet.

items.title: High beams: dim within 500 feet
items.simple: On dark highways, you can use high beams. A car is coming toward you? When it gets within 500 feet, switch to low beams.
items.official: Use high-beam headlights on highways, unless another vehicle is within 500 feet coming toward you.
items.mnemonic: Behind a car: 200 feet. Car coming at you: 500 feet.

items.title: Bright oncoming lights: look aside
items.simple: A car coming at you has bright high beams? Don't stare at the lights. Glance at the side of the road, then look ahead. Repeat until you pass. Keep your own high beams off.
items.official: If the high-beams of an oncoming car are on, avoid looking directly at the bright lights. Glance toward the side of the road, then look quickly ahead to determine the other vehicle's position. Keep doing this until you have passed the other vehicle. Even if the other driver does not dim his headlights, do not turn on your high-beam headlights.

items.title: Fog: low beams, edge, slow
items.simple: Fog bounces light back into your eyes. Use low beams, not high beams. Follow the lines at the edge of the road. Even light fog makes distance hard to judge, so slow down.
items.official: Fog reflects light and can reflect your own headlights back into your eyes. Use low-beam headlights in heavy fog and look for road edge markings to guide you. Even light fog reduces visibility and your ability to judge distances, so slow down.
items.mnemonic: Fog: go low, find the edge, go slow.

items.title: Rain: low beams, check blind spots
items.simple: Heavy rain can be as risky as fog, more so when it is windy. Cars behind you and in your blind spots are hard to see. Use low beams to see and be seen.
items.official: Driving in heavy rain can be as hazardous as driving in fog, especially if the wind is blowing. Other vehicles to the rear and in blind spot areas are especially difficult to see when it's raining. Use your low-beam headlights to see and be seen.

items.title: Wipers and washer fluid
items.simple: In light rain or drizzle, turn on your wipers to see better. Wipers on just a few sprinkles can smear the glass. Keep washer fluid in your car.
items.official: In light rain or drizzle, turn on your windshield wipers to improve visibility; using wipers for sprinkles may smear the windshield and make it harder to see, so make sure you have windshield washer fluid.

items.title: First half hour of rain
items.simple: Rain just started? The road is extra slippery for the first half hour. Oil on the road mixes with the water. Slow down and take care.
items.official: When rain begins, during the first half-hour, roads are more likely to be slippery due to oil on the road surface mixing with water.
items.mnemonic: First 30 minutes of rain: oil slick.

items.title: Avoid ponded water
items.simple: Standing water on the road can make your car hydroplane (slide on the water). You can lose control. Go around it if you can. If you can't, take care.
items.official: Use caution when driving through ponded water, and avoid it if possible. Ponded water can cause vehicles to hydroplane or otherwise lose control.

items.title: Clear all snow before driving
items.simple: Before you drive, clear snow and ice off your whole car. That means roof, hood, back, windows, mirrors and lights. Snow that flies off is a danger to others. Snow tires or chains help stop skids.
items.official: Remove snow and ice from your entire car, including the roof, hood and rear of the vehicle, before you start driving. Snow and ice left on the car can fly off and create a hazard for other motorists. Clear all of your windows, mirrors and front and rear lights. Equip your car with all-weather snow tires or chains to help prevent skidding and reduce stopping distance.

items.title: Ice or packed snow: brake gently
items.simple: Packed snow is like ice. To stop, take your foot off the gas. Then brake gently. Slow down before you stop or turn. Your front tires grip best while they keep rolling.
items.official: Driving on packed snow is similar to driving on ice. When you brake, apply the brakes gently. Slow down before stopping or turning. When driving on slippery surfaces and you need to stop, release the accelerator and apply brakes gently. You have the most traction and control when the front tires are rolling. Keeping a slow, steady speed, rather than hard braking, will allow you to control your vehicle.
items.mnemonic: On ice: gentle feet, rolling wheels.

items.title: Bridges freeze first
items.simple: Bridges freeze before other parts of the road. Shady spots can have ice too. In cold weather, slow down before a bridge.
items.official: Watch for ice on bridges and in shady areas. Bridges freeze before other road surfaces.

items.title: Deer: dusk and dawn, fall
items.simple: Watch for deer at dusk and dawn, most of all in the fall. A deer crossing sign means deer cross here. Slow down and be ready to stop.
items.official: Be alert at dusk and dawn especially in the fall. Deer Crossing: Deer cross the roadway in this area. Slow down, be alert and be ready to stop.
items.mnemonic: Deer at dusk, dawn and fall.

items.title: Deer near road: slow, honk
items.simple: See a deer near the road? Slow down. Deer often travel in groups, so more are likely nearby. Use your horn to scare it away.
items.official: Slow down if you see a large animal near or crossing the road. Large animals frequently travel in groups; there are likely others nearby. Use the horn to scare the animal away.

items.title: Can't miss the deer? Don't swerve
items.simple: Can't miss a deer? Do not swerve. Brake firmly, stay in your lane and come to a controlled stop. If you hit it, tell the police.
items.official: If a collision with a deer or other animal is unavoidable, do not swerve. Brake firmly, stay in your lane, and come to a controlled stop. If you hit a large animal, report it to law enforcement.

items.title: Crash: stop, clear the road
items.simple: In a crash, you must stop at the scene or close to it. Don't block traffic. No one hurt and the cars can move? Move them off the road. Get out with care.
items.official: Stop at the scene of the crash or as close to the scene as possible without blocking traffic. Drivers must move vehicles from the road immediately if the vehicles are able to be moved, no one is injured and the driver is capable of safely doing so. Be careful when exiting your vehicle. Keep your vehicle between you and moving traffic if possible.

items.title: Help the injured, don't move them
items.simple: Help anyone who is hurt in any way you can. Do not pull them out of the car. Move them only if there is danger, like fire, or you have medical training.
items.official: Give any help you can if someone is injured. Do not attempt to move an injured person from a wrecked vehicle unless you have the necessary medical training or there is an immediate danger such as fire.

items.title: Report crashes to police
items.simple: Tell the police about a crash as soon as you can. You must report any crash with damage, injury or death.
items.official: Report the crash to the police as quickly as possible. Motor vehicle crashes involving property damage, personal injury or death must be reported to the police.

items.title: Swap info, call your insurance
items.simple: After a crash, swap info. Get each driver's name, address, license number and plate number. Get names and addresses of anyone hurt and of witnesses. Get owners' insurance. Then call your insurance.
items.official: Exchange information with other people involved in the crash as soon as possible: name, address and driver's license number of other drivers; license plate numbers of other vehicles; name and address of anyone who was injured; name and address of each witness; name, address and insurance policy number of other vehicle owners. Notify your insurance company immediately.

items.title: DMV crash report: over $3,000
items.simple: Police must send a written crash report to DMV if anyone is hurt or killed. They also send one if damage is more than $3,000. The crash goes on each driver's record.
items.official: Law enforcement officers are required to forward a written crash report to DMV when a traffic crash results in injury or the death of any person or total property damage is in excess of $3,000. All crash information will be recorded on the DMV records of each driver involved in the crash.
items.mnemonic: Hurt, killed, or over $3,000: DMV gets a report.

items.title: Parked car hit: note, report
items.simple: Did you hit a parked car with no one in it? Try to find the owner. Can't? Leave a note: your name, phone, date, time and the damage. Tell police within 24 hours.
items.official: You must make a reasonable effort to find the owner of an unattended vehicle or other property damaged in a crash. If you cannot locate anyone, leave a note that can be found easily at the scene of the crash. Include your name, telephone number, the date and time of the crash, and a description of the damage. You must also report the crash to the police within 24 hours.
items.mnemonic: No owner? Leave a note. Tell police within 24 hours.

items.title: Police stop: pull over, stay in
items.simple: Police stopping you? Stay calm. Pull to the side of the road in a safe place and park. Stay in your car unless the officer asks you to get out.
items.official: If you are stopped by a police officer: Remain calm. Pull your vehicle to the side of the road in a safe location and park. Stay in your vehicle. Do not get out unless the officer asks you to.

items.title: Police stop: flashers, inside light
items.simple: After you pull over for police, turn on your flashers. At night, also turn on the light inside your car.
items.official: Turn on your flashers. If you are pulled over at night, turn on your vehicle's interior lights.

items.title: Police stop: engine off, window down
items.simple: Turn off your engine and radio. Turn off anything that makes it hard to talk. Roll down your window. The officer may walk up on either side of your car.
items.official: Turn off your engine, radio, and any other device that could block communication with the officer. Roll down your window so that you can communicate with the officer. An officer may approach your vehicle on the driver or passenger side for safety reasons.

items.title: Police stop: belts on, hands seen
items.simple: Keep your seat belt on. Keep your hands on the wheel where the officer can see them. Don't reach around. Asked for papers? Say where they are. Reach slowly, one hand on the wheel.
items.official: Keep your safety belt fastened and ask your passengers to keep their belts fastened. Keep your hands in plain view, preferably on the steering wheel. Ask your passengers to keep their hands in plain view also. Do not make any movement that will make the officer think you are hiding or reaching for something. If the officer asks for your license, registration and insurance documents, tell him where they are and reach for them slowly, keeping one hand on the steering wheel.

items.title: Carry license, registration, insurance
items.simple: Always carry three things when you drive. You need your driver's license and proof your car is registered. You also need proof of insurance. An officer may ask to see them.
items.official: Carry proper identification: a valid driver's license, proof of vehicle registration and proof of insurance.
items.mnemonic: 3 papers: you (license), your car (registration), your coverage (insurance).

items.title: Unmarked car: ask for ID
items.simple: Is the officer in an unmarked car? Not in uniform? You may ask to see the officer's ID.
items.official: If the officer is driving an unmarked car or is not in uniform, you may ask to see his or her identification.

items.title: Sign the ticket; argue in court
items.simple: Answer the officer's questions clearly. Disagree? Don't argue now. You can make your case in court. Sign the ticket. Signing does not mean you admit guilt.
items.official: Answer the officer's questions fully and clearly. If you disagree with the officer, do not discuss your point of view at that time. You will have your chance to make your case in court. Sign the citation; this is not an admission of guilt. Refusal to sign the citation may result in your arrest. Or, you may be required to go to the police station.

questions.explain: Switch to low beams whenever you meet oncoming traffic so you do not blind the other driver.

questions.prompt: You dim your headlights for oncoming traffic in order to:
questions.explain: Switch to low beams for oncoming traffic to avoid blinding the other driver.

questions.prompt: When following another vehicle at night, use low beams when you are within:
questions.explain: When following, use low beams whenever you are within 200 feet of the vehicle ahead.

questions.prompt: You are driving at night and come within 200 feet of the vehicle ahead. You should:
questions.explain: Use low beams when you are within 200 feet of the vehicle you are following.

questions.prompt: On a highway at night, you must dim your high beams when an oncoming vehicle is within:
questions.explain: Use high beams on highways unless an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet.

questions.prompt: High-beam headlights should be used:
choices: In cities and towns on lighted streets
On highways, unless an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet
questions.explain: Use high beams on highways, unless another vehicle is within 500 feet coming toward you.

questions.prompt: You are using high beams on a dark highway. A car coming toward you is less than 500 feet away. You should:
questions.explain: Dim to low beams when an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet.

questions.prompt: If an oncoming driver has high beams on, you should:
choices: Look directly at the oncoming lights
Turn on your own high beams
Glance toward the side of the road, then look quickly ahead
Stop in your lane until the car passes
questions.explain: Avoid looking at the bright lights; glance toward the side of the road, then look quickly ahead.

questions.prompt: An oncoming driver does not dim his high beams. You should:
choices: Turn on your high beams to warn him
Flash your high beams until he dims
questions.explain: Even if the other driver does not dim his headlights, do not turn on your high beams.

questions.prompt: When glare from an oncoming car's high beams bothers you, keep glancing toward the side of the road and then ahead until:
choices: You have passed the other vehicle
questions.explain: Glance aside, then quickly ahead, and keep doing this until you have passed the other vehicle.

questions.prompt: When driving in heavy fog, you should use:
questions.explain: Use low-beam headlights in heavy fog.

questions.prompt: In heavy fog, what should you look for to guide you?
choices: The taillights of the car ahead
questions.explain: In heavy fog, look for road edge markings to guide you.

questions.prompt: You should slow down even in light fog because:
choices: Fog reduces visibility and your ability to judge distances
Fog makes your engine run hot
questions.explain: Even light fog reduces visibility and your ability to judge distances, so slow down.

questions.prompt: High-beam headlights are a poor choice in fog because:
choices: Fog reflects your own light back into your eyes
They make your car harder to see
questions.explain: Fog reflects light and can reflect your own headlights back into your eyes.

questions.prompt: When driving in rain, you should use:
questions.explain: Use your low-beam headlights in rain to see and be seen.

questions.prompt: When it is raining, which vehicles are especially hard to see?
choices: Vehicles directly in front of you
Vehicles to the rear and in blind spot areas
Vehicles stopped at a red light
questions.explain: Vehicles to the rear and in blind spot areas are especially difficult to see in rain.

questions.prompt: Driving in heavy rain can be as hazardous as driving in fog, especially when:
choices: You are on a city street
questions.explain: Heavy rain can be as hazardous as fog, especially if the wind is blowing.

questions.prompt: Using wipers for only a few sprinkles may smear the windshield, so you should:
choices: Never use wipers in light rain
Make sure you have windshield washer fluid
questions.explain: Wipers used for sprinkles may smear the windshield, so make sure you have washer fluid.

questions.prompt: In light rain or drizzle, you should:
choices: Wait for heavy rain before using wipers
Turn on your windshield wipers to improve visibility
questions.explain: In light rain or drizzle, turn on your windshield wipers to improve visibility.

questions.prompt: When rain begins, roads are more likely to be slippery during the first:
questions.explain: During the first half-hour of rain, roads are more likely to be slippery.

questions.prompt: Roads are more slippery right after rain begins because:
choices: Oil on the road surface mixes with water
questions.explain: Oil on the road surface mixes with water when rain begins.

questions.prompt: You see this sign and rain has just begun. You should:
choices: Speed up to get out of the rain
Slow down; the road may be extra slippery
Brake hard to test the road
questions.explain: This sign warns that the road is slippery, and roads are more likely to be slippery in the first half-hour of rain.

questions.prompt: Ponded water on the road can cause your vehicle to:
questions.explain: Ponded water can cause vehicles to hydroplane or otherwise lose control.

questions.prompt: When you see ponded water on the road, you should:
choices: Speed up to get through it quickly
Brake hard in the middle of it
Avoid it if possible, or use caution
questions.explain: Use caution when driving through ponded water, and avoid it if possible.

questions.prompt: Before driving after a snowfall, you should remove snow and ice from:
choices: Your entire car, including roof, hood, rear, windows, mirrors and lights
Only the front and rear lights
questions.explain: Remove snow and ice from your entire car before you start driving.

questions.prompt: All-weather snow tires or chains help:
choices: Prevent skidding and reduce stopping distance
Make it safe to follow closely
Replace the need to slow down
questions.explain: Snow tires or chains help prevent skidding and reduce stopping distance.

questions.prompt: Why should you clear snow off your roof before driving?
choices: It can fly off and create a hazard for other drivers
It is needed to open your doors
questions.explain: Snow and ice left on the car can fly off and create a hazard for other motorists.

questions.prompt: If you are driving on an icy or slippery road and have to stop, you should:
choices: Apply the brakes in a normal way
Release the gas and apply the brakes gently
questions.explain: On slippery surfaces, release the accelerator and apply the brakes gently.

questions.prompt: On slippery surfaces, you have the most traction and control when your front tires are:
questions.explain: You have the most traction and control when the front tires are rolling.

questions.prompt: Driving on packed snow is similar to driving on:
questions.explain: Driving on packed snow is similar to driving on ice.

questions.prompt: On a slippery road, what helps you control your vehicle best?
questions.explain: A slow, steady speed, rather than hard braking, lets you control your vehicle.

questions.prompt: Which road surface freezes before other road surfaces?
questions.explain: Bridges freeze before other road surfaces.

questions.prompt: In freezing weather, you should watch for ice especially:
choices: On bridges and in shady areas
questions.explain: Watch for ice on bridges and in shady areas.

questions.prompt: You see this sign at dusk in the fall. You should:
choices: Speed up to get past the area
Slow down, be alert and be ready to stop
Use the shoulder to drive around animals
questions.explain: Deer cross in this area; slow down, be alert and be ready to stop, especially at dusk and dawn in the fall.

questions.prompt: You should be especially alert for deer and other large animals:
choices: At dusk and dawn, especially in the fall
questions.explain: Be alert at dusk and dawn, especially in the fall.

questions.prompt: You see a deer cross the road ahead. You should:
choices: Speed up before more deer come
Slow down because others are likely nearby
Stop and get out of your car
questions.explain: Slow down; large animals often travel in groups, so others are likely nearby.

questions.prompt: To scare a deer or other large animal away from the road, you can:
questions.explain: Use the horn to scare the animal away.

questions.prompt: You pass this sign and one deer runs across the road. You should expect:
choices: The deer to stay off the road
questions.explain: Large animals frequently travel in groups, so there are likely others nearby.

questions.prompt: If a collision with a deer is unavoidable, you should:
choices: Swerve into the next lane to miss it
Speed up to get past it
Brake firmly, stay in your lane and come to a controlled stop
questions.explain: Do not swerve; brake firmly, stay in your lane and come to a controlled stop.

questions.prompt: If you hit a large animal, you should:
choices: Report it only if your car is damaged
questions.explain: If you hit a large animal, report it to law enforcement.

questions.prompt: If you are involved in a crash, you must:
choices: Take the injured person to the nearest hospital
Continue home and file a crash report
Stop, help any injured, report the crash to the police, exchange information and notify your insurance company
Check your car for damage and leave
questions.explain: After a crash you must stop, help the injured, report to police, exchange information and notify your insurance company.

questions.prompt: After a crash where no one is hurt and the vehicles can be moved, drivers must:
choices: Move the vehicles from the road immediately if they can do so safely
Leave the vehicles where they are until police arrive
questions.explain: Drivers must move vehicles from the road immediately if they can be moved, no one is injured and it is safe.

questions.prompt: When you get out of your car after a crash, you should:
choices: Stand in the lane to warn others
Stand behind your car in the lane
Keep your vehicle between you and moving traffic if possible
questions.explain: Be careful exiting, and keep your vehicle between you and moving traffic if possible.

questions.prompt: You should not move an injured person from a wrecked vehicle unless:
choices: You want to drive them home
There is an immediate danger, such as fire, or you have medical training
questions.explain: Do not move an injured person unless you have medical training or there is an immediate danger such as fire.

questions.prompt: At a crash scene where someone is injured, you should:
choices: Pull the person out of the car right away
Move the person into your car
Give any help you can, without moving them unless there is immediate danger
questions.explain: Give any help you can, but do not move an injured person unless there is immediate danger or you are trained.

questions.prompt: Crashes involving property damage, personal injury or death:
choices: Do not need to be reported
Only need to be reported to your insurance
Must be reported to the police
Must be reported only if someone is killed
questions.explain: Crashes involving property damage, personal injury or death must be reported to the police.

questions.prompt: If you are involved in a traffic crash, you must report it to the police:
choices: Only if the other driver asks
Only if your car cannot be driven
questions.explain: Report the crash to the police as quickly as possible.

questions.prompt: After a crash, you should get the following from the other drivers:
choices: Name, address and driver's license number
questions.explain: Get the name, address and driver's license number of other drivers.

questions.prompt: From the owners of the other vehicles in a crash, you should get their:
choices: Name, address and insurance policy number
questions.explain: Get the name, address and insurance policy number of other vehicle owners.

questions.prompt: After a crash, you should notify your insurance company:
choices: Only if you were at fault
Only if police tell you to
questions.explain: Notify your insurance company immediately after a crash.

questions.prompt: Officers must send a written crash report to DMV when total property damage is more than:
questions.explain: A written crash report goes to DMV when property damage is over $3,000, or someone is injured or killed.

questions.prompt: Crash information is recorded on:
choices: Only the record of the driver at fault
The DMV records of each driver involved
No DMV record unless someone is hurt
questions.explain: All crash information is recorded on the DMV records of each driver involved.

questions.prompt: A law enforcement officer must forward a written crash report to DMV when a crash results in:
choices: Injury or death of any person
questions.explain: Officers forward a crash report to DMV for injury, death, or property damage over $3,000.

questions.prompt: If you damage an unattended vehicle and cannot find the owner, you must leave a note and report the crash to the police within:
questions.explain: You must report the crash to the police within 24 hours.

questions.prompt: A note left on an unattended vehicle you damaged must include:
choices: Your name, telephone number, the date and time of the crash, and a description of the damage
questions.explain: Include your name, phone number, the date and time of the crash, and a description of the damage.

questions.prompt: If you hit a parked car and no one is around, you must first:
choices: Drive away if the damage is small
Make a reasonable effort to find the owner
questions.explain: You must make a reasonable effort to find the owner of an unattended vehicle you damage.

questions.prompt: If you are stopped by a police officer, you should:
choices: Get out and walk to the police car
Stay in your vehicle unless the officer asks you to get out
questions.explain: Stay in your vehicle; do not get out unless the officer asks you to.

questions.prompt: When a police officer signals you to stop, you should:
choices: Remain calm and pull to the side of the road in a safe location
Speed up to find a parking lot
questions.explain: Remain calm, pull to the side of the road in a safe location and park.

questions.prompt: If you are pulled over by police at night, you should:
choices: Turn on your vehicle's interior lights
questions.explain: If you are pulled over at night, turn on your vehicle's interior lights.

questions.prompt: After pulling over for a police officer, you should turn on your:
questions.explain: Turn on your flashers when you are stopped by a police officer.

questions.prompt: During a traffic stop, you should:
choices: Keep your engine and radio on
Turn off your engine, radio and other devices
questions.explain: Turn off your engine, radio and any device that could block communication with the officer.

questions.prompt: Why should you roll down your window during a traffic stop?
choices: So the officer can reach your keys
questions.explain: Roll down your window so that you can communicate with the officer.

questions.prompt: During a traffic stop, the officer may approach your vehicle:
choices: On the driver or passenger side
questions.explain: An officer may approach on the driver or passenger side for safety reasons.

questions.prompt: During a traffic stop, keep your hands:
choices: In plain view, preferably on the steering wheel
questions.explain: Keep your hands in plain view, preferably on the steering wheel.

questions.prompt: When an officer asks for your license, registration and proof of insurance, you should:
choices: Tell the officer where they are and reach slowly, keeping one hand on the wheel
Quickly dig through your glove box
Get out and look in the trunk
questions.explain: Tell the officer where the documents are and reach for them slowly, keeping one hand on the steering wheel.

questions.prompt: During a traffic stop, you and your passengers should:
questions.explain: Keep your safety belt fastened and ask passengers to keep theirs fastened.

questions.prompt: During a traffic stop, your passengers should:
choices: Keep their hands in plain view
Get out to talk to the officer
questions.explain: Ask your passengers to keep their hands in plain view and their belts fastened.

questions.prompt: When you drive, you should carry:
choices: Your license and your car title
A valid driver's license, proof of vehicle registration and proof of insurance
questions.explain: Carry a valid driver's license, proof of vehicle registration and proof of insurance.

questions.prompt: A police officer stops you and asks for your documents. Which should you have with you?
choices: Your license, registration and proof of insurance
questions.explain: Carry proper identification: a valid driver's license, proof of vehicle registration and proof of insurance.

questions.prompt: If the officer who stops you is driving an unmarked car or is not in uniform, you may:
choices: Ask to see his or her identification
questions.explain: If the officer is in an unmarked car or not in uniform, you may ask to see identification.

questions.prompt: You may ask to see a police officer's identification when the officer:
choices: Is driving an unmarked car or is not in uniform
Is in uniform in a marked car
questions.explain: You may ask for identification if the officer is in an unmarked car or not in uniform.

questions.prompt: Signing a traffic citation:
choices: Is not an admission of guilt
Is optional and has no effect
Means you must pay right away
questions.explain: Sign the citation; this is not an admission of guilt.

questions.prompt: Refusing to sign a traffic citation may result in:
questions.explain: Refusal to sign the citation may result in your arrest.

questions.prompt: If you disagree with the officer during a traffic stop, you should:
choices: Argue your point of view right away
Wait and make your case in court
questions.explain: Do not discuss your point of view at the stop; you will have your chance in court.
